author: Carlos Martinez
title: iRacing on Mac: The realistic options and trade-offs
description: iRacing doesn't run natively on macOS. Here's what actually works, what doesn't, and what the performance cost really is.

sections.p: The first thing I tell someone asking if they can run iRacing on their Mac is this: iRacing is Windows-only software. No native macOS build exists, and Sim Innovations (the company behind iRacing) has never committed to building one. That's the starting point for any honest conversation about Mac and sim racing.

I say this because I see a lot of people online suggesting workarounds that sound plausible but deliver mediocre results or quiet disappointment. If you own a Mac and want to race on iRacing, you have real options, but they all involve trade-offs. I'll walk through them from most practical to least practical, based on what I've seen work and fail in the sim racing community.

sections.h2: Bootcamp (Intel Macs only, but mostly deprecated)

sections.p: If you're still running an Intel-based Mac, Bootcamp is a native dual-boot solution that lets you install Windows directly on your hardware. This is the cleanest approach for Intel machines because there's no emulation layer, no translation overhead. You reboot into Windows, iRacing runs as if you were on a Windows PC, and FFB works reliably.

The catch: Bootcamp only works on Intel Macs, and Apple discontinued it with the transition to Apple Silicon (M1, M2, M3, and later chips). If you bought a Mac in the last three years, you have an Apple Silicon chip. Bootcamp is off the table.

For Intel Mac owners still using older machines, Bootcamp remains solid. But I'd take a hard look at your hardware's age and gaming capability before sinking time into it. An older Intel Mac might have throttling issues or a weak GPU that makes iRacing frustrating anyway.

sections.h2: Parallels Desktop (Apple Silicon Macs, ARM translation)

sections.p: Parallels Desktop is a hypervisor that runs Windows ARM natively on Apple Silicon Macs. It's elegant on paper: you keep your Mac environment, spin up a Windows virtual machine, and launch iRacing inside that VM. Many professional tools work well this way.

But iRacing on Parallels is a disappointment in practice. Here's why: iRacing requires direct access to your GPU's VRAM and uses low-level graphics APIs (DirectX 11). Parallels abstracts both of these. Your GPU performance is throttled. Multiplayer servers sometimes reject the connection because they detect non-native Windows. Force feedback from my MOZA R9 wheelbase either doesn't work or works intermittently depending on the Parallels version and Windows ARM build you're running.

I've heard from racers who got Parallels working, but every single one reported noticeably lower frame rates (40-60% performance loss is typical), consistent FFB issues, and frequent disconnections from servers. It's not a solution for serious racing. It's a temporary curiosity.

sections.tip: Parallels Desktop also costs ~$100/year for updates and licensing. When the experience is already compromised, paying for that overhead makes it harder to justify.

sections.h2: UTM or other free hypervisors (worse than Parallels)

sections.p: UTM is a free, open-source hypervisor for macOS. Some people suggest it as a budget alternative to Parallels. Don't. UTM's GPU passthrough and graphics translation are even more limited than Parallels. iRacing runs slower, looks worse, and the chance of FFB working at all is near zero.

There are other options (Fusion, etc.), but they all share the same fundamental problem: virtualization adds overhead that sim racing, with its real-time input and FFB requirements, simply cannot tolerate. A 60 Hz steering wheel input should arrive within milliseconds. Virtualization adds latency and unpredictability.

sections.h2: External Windows PC or gaming laptop (the real solution)

sections.p: If you're serious about iRacing and you own a Mac, the honest answer is to use a separate Windows PC or gaming laptop for racing. This is not elegant. It means keeping two computers around. But it's the only approach that delivers the experience iRacing is designed for.

This can range from an older gaming laptop you find second-hand for ~$500-800 to a purpose-built racing PC. If you're willing to go used, you can get a machine capable of running iRacing smoothly at 1440p 120 Hz or VR without much spending. I built a dedicated racing box a few years back using older components, and it cost far less than upgrading my Mac and dealing with a year of virtualization headaches.

The practical setup: Mac for everything else, gaming PC parked next to your sim rig, wired to your monitor and steering wheel. It's two machines, yes, but each one does one job well. My MOZA R9 wheelbase, MOZA CRP2 pedals, and fixed cockpit all plug into the Windows racing PC. Full compatibility, full FFB, no compromises.

list: Used gaming laptops (RTX 3060 or better) often sell for ~$600-900 and handle iRacing at high settings.
Older desktop towers with a GTX 1080 or RTX 2070 are even cheaper on the second-hand market and run cooler under load.
Even a budget new build with a GPU like an RTX 4060 or 4070 will outperform any virtualized option and cost less than Parallels frustration.
Wired Ethernet and a USB hub make peripheral setup simple and latency-free.

sections.h2: Cloud gaming and remote desktop (not for sim racing)

sections.p: Some people ask about cloud-based solutions or remote desktop software like Steam Link or Parsec. Technically, you could run iRacing on a remote Windows PC and stream it back to your Mac. Latency kills the experience. Steering wheel FFB becomes mushy and delayed. Braking input lag becomes noticeable. For a time trial, you might not care. For league racing, it's uncompetitive.
Cloud gaming services like GeForce Now or Xbox Cloud Gaming don't offer iRacing at all (iRacing isn't available on any major cloud platform). So this door is closed.

If I were an iRacing-focused Mac owner right now, I'd buy a used gaming laptop or small form-factor Windows desktop for ~$500-700, plug my MOZA R9, CRP2 pedals, and cockpit into it, and call it done. Total cost: less than a year's worth of fighting Parallels. Total frustration: zero.

This assumes you're serious about racing. If you're just curious about iRacing and want to test drive it without much investment, renting time at a local sim racing venue might be worth exploring. Many offer hourly session access on real rigs. You avoid the Mac problem entirely and get a feel for whether competitive sim racing is worth the commitment.

macOS is excellent at a lot of things. Running Windows-exclusive racing software natively is not one of them, and no workaround will change that. The sooner you accept that and plan around it, the sooner you can actually race.

faqs.q: Can I run iRacing on Apple Silicon Mac with Bootcamp?
faqs.a: No. Apple discontinued Bootcamp with the transition to Apple Silicon chips (M1 and later). Bootcamp only works on Intel Macs, which are now several years old. If you have an M1, M2, M3, or newer Mac, Bootcamp is not an option.

faqs.q: Will iRacing work on Parallels Desktop?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but with severe compromises. Parallels translates Windows ARM to run on Apple Silicon, and this translation overhead reduces iRacing's frame rate by 40-60%. Force feedback is unreliable or non-functional, and multiplayer servers sometimes reject your connection. It's not a reliable racing solution.

faqs.q: What's the best realistic option for Mac owners who want to race iRacing?
faqs.a: Buy or borrow a used Windows gaming PC or laptop (budget around 500-800 dollars for a machine capable of running iRacing at good settings). Plug your sim rig peripherals into the Windows machine. This avoids all virtualization overhead and gives you full compatibility with FFB and the iRacing client.

faqs.q: Can I use cloud gaming or remote desktop to play iRacing on my Mac?
faqs.a: Cloud-based iRacing is not available through any major cloud platform. Remote desktop or game streaming adds latency that makes real-time input (steering and braking) feel delayed and unresponsive. It's uncompetitive for actual racing, especially with a load-cell wheelbase where FFB and responsiveness matter.
